title: Games and Norms
subtitle: From cultural evolution to institutions
description: A self-paced course: why humans cooperate, how strategic interaction works, and how norms, networks and institutions turn it into order.
tagline: Learn what 11 books know about cooperation, then design it into a real group.
lede: Three levels, in order: where human sociality comes from, the psychology and game theory of interaction, and how norms, institutions and networks produce collective order. Then a critical look at one attempt to unify it all. Every decision you make about your own group goes into your cooperation brief, labeled as evidence, hypothesis, or value.
artifact_lede: One document about a real group you choose: a team, a community, a platform, a commons. It grows with every module.
artifact_critique_prompt: Critique this cooperation brief. Check: (1) tagging discipline: anything tagged [E] that is really [H] or [V], or vice versa; (2) contradictions with what the course teaches (the game structure must be diagnosed before the fix; norms need both empirical and normative expectations; Ostrom's design principles; network structure shapes diffusion and cascades; social preferences are real but conditional; risk-dominance beats payoff-dominance under uncertainty); (3) internal inconsistencies between sections; (4) the single most important missing decision. Be direct.
case_lede: Realistic situations you hit when trying to get a team, community, platform or commons to cooperate.
model_lede: Read it like a building: cultural evolution is the foundation at the bottom, and each band constrains the one above it. Certainty drops as you go up: the formal results are theorems; the institutional prescriptions are mostly hypothesis and value.
mentor_voice: You are a demanding but supportive mentor (high standards, high support) coaching a learner who is trying to design cooperation into a real group: a team, a community, a platform or a commons. They have a software/product background. Be specific and concise (under 250 words). Use markdown bullets. Tag design claims as [E] evidence, [H] hypothesis, [V] value where useful.

tags.H: hypothesis to test in your group
